slides.title: How Tight Is the Scatter Plot?
slides.alt: A scatter diagram of twenty points rising in a tight cloud

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the scatter plot? · The situation
slides.title: Revision and marks

setup.preamble: A teacher wonders whether students who revise more score higher on the unit test.
setup.para: She asks 20 students how many hours they revise each week, $h$, and records each test mark out of $100$, $m$. Every student is one point on a scatter diagram.

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the scatter plot? · Question 1
slides.title: Read the cloud
slides.stem: Predict: which value of $r$ matches this scatter diagram?

walk.cap: The points hug a rising line
walk.note: $r$ is Pearson’s product-moment correlation coefficient. It measures how close the points lie to a straight line, and the GDC finds it. A value near $1$ means a tight, rising, straight pattern.

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the scatter plot? · Question 1
slides.title: A scale for $|r|$
slides.stem: How do we put a word on the size of $r$? Use $|r|$, the size without the sign.

walk.note: The sign gives the direction: $+$ rises, $-$ falls. This scatter is a very strong positive linear correlation.

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the scatter plot? · Question 2
slides.title: Spread the points
slides.stem: A second school finds the same trend, but the points are more spread out. Predict what happens to $r$.

walk.note: $r$ falls as the points spread out. It stays positive because the trend still rises.

slides.eyebrow: How tight is the scatter plot? · Question 3
slides.title: Read the line
slides.stem: The GDC line is $m=4.02h+18.3$. What do the slope and the intercept mean here?

walk.note: Each extra hour of revision a week goes with about $4$ more marks.
About $18$ marks with no revision. That is sensible: the data start near $0$ hours.

slides.eyebrow: Mathematician · University College London
slides.name: Karl Pearson

blocks.head: The question
blocks.text: How strongly are children’s heights tied to their parents’? Francis Galton had the data and the first idea. Pearson, his colleague, wanted exact mathematics for heredity.

blocks.head: The work
blocks.text: He turned Galton’s slope into a formula: the average product of each point’s deviations from the two means, scaled to run from $-1$ to $1$. That is $r$, and it measures straight lines only.

blocks.head: The hard part
blocks.text: Pearson was a eugenicist. He used correlations to argue that heredity outweighs environment, and that selective breeding, not social reform, should shape the population. One historian judges that this rested more on class prejudice than on sound science.

slides.title: A Curve That Only Goes Up
slides.alt: A plant’s height each week: points rising along an upward curve

slides.eyebrow: A curve that only goes up · The situation
slides.title: A seedling

setup.preamble: A gardener measures a seedling at the end of each week.
setup.para: Over 10 weeks she records $w$, the week number, and $H$, the height in centimetres. The plant is taller every week than the week before.

facts.html: 10 weeks of heights: one point each

slides.eyebrow: A curve that only goes up · Question 1
slides.title: Always rising
slides.stem: Predict: the plant rises every week. What is $r$?

walk.note: Always rising: monotonic increasing. Always falling: monotonic decreasing. Pearson’s $r$ rewards straight lines, so it stays below $1$.

slides.eyebrow: A curve that only goes up · Question 2
slides.title: Read the line
slides.stem: The GDC line is $H=3.03w-7.77$. What do the slope and the intercept mean here?

walk.note: On average the plant grows about $3$ cm each week.
A height of $-7.77$ cm is impossible. The line only fits the weeks measured, not week $0$.

slides.eyebrow: A curve that only goes up · Question 3
slides.title: One odd point
slides.stem: A sensor glitch records the plant at only $5$ cm in week 11. Predict what happens to $r$.

walk.note: One unusual point, an outlier, can drag $r$ a long way.

slides.eyebrow: A curve that only goes up · Drag the outlier
slides.title: One point and Pearson’s product-moment correlation coefficient

slides.eyebrow: Psychologist · University College London
slides.name: Charles Spearman

blocks.head: The question
blocks.text: Are pupils who do well in one school subject good at the others? Does cleverness show in simple senses such as hearing pitch? In 1904 he was working toward a PhD in Leipzig under Wilhelm Wundt and set out to measure it.

blocks.head: The work
blocks.text: His data were often rankings, such as a teacher’s ordering of pupils, so he built a coefficient for two rankings. Today $r_s$ is Pearson’s $r$ computed on the ranks.

blocks.head: On your calculator
blocks.text: $r_s=1$ when one ranking rises exactly as the other does, even along a curve. So $r_s$ measures how monotonic a relationship is, where Pearson’s $r$ measures how linear.

slides.title: Eight Sprinters
slides.alt: Eight athletes: a rising scatter that levels off

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · The situation
slides.title: Training and improvement

setup.preamble: A coach follows eight sprinters through a season.
setup.para: For each athlete she records $h$, the hours of training each week, and $t$, how many seconds faster the athlete runs 100 m. More training helps, but the gains slow down: the points rise without lying on a straight line. Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, $r_s$, measures how monotonic they are.

facts.html: $t$: improvement in 100 m time, in seconds

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · Question 1
slides.title: Rank by hand
slides.stem: Rank $h$ and $t$, smallest first. What rank do the two tied athletes get?

walk.note: The tie takes places 3 and 4, so each gets $\frac{3+4}{2}=3.5$.

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · Question 2
slides.title: Which is closer to 1?
slides.stem: Next the GDC finds Pearson’s $r$ for the data, then Spearman’s $r_s$ for the ranks. Predict which is closer to $1$.

walk.note: First $r$ for the data, then $r_s$ for the ranks.

slides.title: Find $r$ for the data
slides.stem: Hours $h$ are in List 1 and improvements $t$ in List 2.

start.alt: List 1 holds the hours and List 2 the improvements

steps.t: Press [F6] SET. 2Var XList is List 1 and 2Var YList is List 2.

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · Question 3
slides.title: Read the line
slides.stem: The GDC line is $t=0.0575h+0.148$. What do the slope and the intercept mean here?

walk.note: Each extra hour of training goes with about $0.06$ s more improvement.
About $0.15$ s with no training. Nobody trained under $2$ hours, so treat this with care.

slides.title: Find $r_s$ from the ranks
slides.stem: Your ranks of $h$ are in List 3 and your ranks of $t$ in List 4. The tied ranks are $3.5$.

start.alt: Ranks entered in List 3 and List 4; the CALC menu is open

steps.t: Press [F6] SET. [DOWN] twice, [F1] LIST, {3} [EXE] for 2Var XList. Then [DOWN], [F1] LIST, {4} [EXE] for 2Var YList.
Press [F1] ax+b. Read $r_s=0.994$ to 3 s.f. Afterwards set SET back to List 1 and List 2.

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · Question 4
slides.title: Plot the ranks
slides.stem: Plot the rank of $t$ against the rank of $h$. How does this scatter compare with the original?

walk.cap: The ranks line up almost perfectly
walk.note: $r_s$ is Pearson’s $r$ applied to the ranks. The ranked points hug a straight line far more closely than the original scatter, so $r_s$ is closer to $1$.

slides.eyebrow: Eight sprinters · Question 5
slides.title: What does $r_s>r$ suggest?
slides.stem: The GDC gives $r=0.935$ and $r_s=0.994$. What does $r_s>r$ suggest?

walk.note: It suggests the data are close to monotonic but not linear, or an outlier is dragging $r$ down. The tied pair keeps $r_s$ just below $1$. Always check the scatter.

choices: A steady rise along a curve

Ice Cream and Sunburn
slides.alt: Twelve months of ice cream sales against sunburn cases: a rising band

slides.eyebrow: Ice cream and sunburn · The situation
slides.title: A coastal town

setup.preamble: A seaside town keeps two records through the year.
setup.para: Each month it notes $I$, the ice creams sold per day, and $S$, the sunburn cases seen at the clinic. That gives 12 points.

slides.eyebrow: Ice cream and sunburn · Question 1
slides.title: Cause?
slides.stem: The scatter has $r=0.99$. Does eating ice cream cause sunburn?

walk.cap: A high $r$ is not a cause
walk.note: Correlation says the variables move together. It never says that one causes the other.

choices: Yes: a high $r$ shows one causes the other
No: they have nothing to do with each other
They move together, but $r$ cannot say why

slides.eyebrow: Ice cream and sunburn · Question 2
slides.title: A third variable
slides.stem: Something else changes through the year. Plot each variable against the monthly temperature, $T$ in °C.

walk.note: Hot months have more ice cream sales and more sunburn: the weather drives both. A third variable can produce a strong $r$ between two things that do not affect each other.
